tip: 'Être en vacances' = to be on vacation. Note the plural 'vacances' – always plural in French.
'Avoir mal à' + body part = to hurt: 'j'ai mal au ventre'. The article contracts: à + le = au.
Time takes an empty 'il' in French, like weather does. Quelle heure est-il ? is literally "what hour is it" – the il stands for nothing, it just holds the verb.
French HAS your age, it doesn't say you ARE it. Quel âge as-tu ? = "what age have you", and you answer j'ai 30 ans, "I have 30 years" – never je suis.
'De l'' is the partitive before vowels: de l'eau, de l'huile, de l'argent. Same meaning as du/de la: 'some'.
There's no one-word "home" here: il est à la maison is literally "at the house". Heading home is rentrer à la maison.
French uses "the" for body parts where English says "his": il a les cheveux noirs is literally "the black hair", not "his black hair".
'Qu'est-ce que' = what (as object). Literally 'What is it that'. Used for asking about things/actions.
In speech, on almost always replaces nous: 'on mange' for 'we eat'. Nous now sounds formal or written.
Weather 'makes' in French: 'il fait beau' is literally 'it makes nice' = it's nice out. Cold and hot too: il fait froid, il fait chaud.
French can't drop the "some": je veux de la viande, never "je veux viande". That de la is required even when English leaves it out and just says "meat".

target: Elle a mal à la tête.
tip: 'Avoir mal à' = to have pain in: j'ai mal au dos (my back hurts), j'ai mal aux dents (I have a toothache).
'Est-ce que' placed before a statement turns it into a yes/no question. It's the most common question form in spoken French.
Negation wraps the verb in two parts: 'ne manges pas'. In casual speech the ne drops – you'll hear tu manges pas – but writing keeps it.
'De quoi' = What...of/about. Use after verbs that take 'de': avoir besoin de, parler de, avoir envie de.

target: Il n'y a pas de pain.
tip: After negation, 'du/de la/des' become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.

target: Est-ce que nous sommes en retard ?
tip: In questions, 'est-ce que nous' sounds natural. The inverted form 'sommes-nous' is more formal.

target: Est-ce que tu as des questions ?
tip: English drops the article in 'any questions', but French keeps it: 'des questions'. Des is the plural of un/une and can't be skipped.
'Avoir hâte de' = to be eager to / can't wait to. Literally 'to have haste to'.
When inverting with il/elle/on, add '-t-' between two vowels for pronunciation: A-t-il ? Va-t-elle ? Mange-t-on ?
'Lequel/laquelle' = Which one. Agrees with the noun: lequel (m.), laquelle (f.), lesquels (m. pl.), lesquelles (f. pl.).
Drop the "a" before jobs: ma mère est professeure, not "une professeure". Same with il est médecin. The article only returns once you add an adjective.

english: I am afraid of the dog.
tip: 'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
'Avoir envie de' = to feel like / to want. J'ai envie d'un café = I feel like having a coffee.
After a question word French can flip the verb and its noun: quand arrive le train ? puts arrive ahead of le train – "when arrives the train".
After negation, 'des' becomes 'd'' before a vowel: 'pas d'amis'. The partitive article disappears.
Before a vowel, vieux becomes vieil: 'un vieil homme', never vieux homme. It's purely to avoid two vowel sounds clashing.

english: How much do I owe you?
tip: Devoir means both "must" and "owe". Combien je vous dois ? = "how much do I owe you" – here it's money owed, not obligation.
Pouvoir turns irregular when you invert it: puis-je, never "peux-je". En quoi puis-je vous aider ? is the polite "how can I help you".

target: Les magasins ferment à vingt heures.
english: The stores close at eight pm.
tip: 'Les magasins' – use 'les' for all/general plural nouns. 'Des' would mean 'some' stores.
